paper.title: ‘Migrant Carer-Wives’ – Between Transnational Marriages, Care Work for Older Husbands and Gendered Precarity
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed and no Statistics Denmark (DST) project reference is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish register data / 'various registers' linked by the unique personal identifier
registers.role: sample frame; treatment (sex, age, country of origin, migration year) and outcome (remarriage, spousal age difference) measurement

linkages: all legal residents in Denmark (both immigrants and natives) are assigned a unique personal identifier which, across various registers, ties together information on gender, age, year of migration, country of origin and years of marriage, divorce and widowhood (p. 161; PDF p. 6)
spouses are linked within a marriage so that the age difference between husband and wife can be computed (implied by the reported age differences, pp. 161-162 (PDF pp. 6-7))

sample.universe: Legal residents of Denmark in the 55- to 80-year age group, 2003-2018; the focus is previously married (widowed or divorced) immigrants from Turkey, from Pakistan, and – pooled – from the four Arab refugee countries Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan, with the Danish majority as comparison
sample.unit_of_observation: individual (person) aged 55-80, with remarriages and the resulting spousal age differences observed over 2003-2018
selection_rules: individuals in the 55- to 80-year age group
previously married: now widows/widowers or divorcees
immigrants from Turkey or Pakistan, or – pooled together – from the four Arab refugee countries of Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan; results compared with the Danish majority
sample.n_individuals: almost 11,000 Turkish immigrants in the 55- to 80-year age group (the only group size the paper prints); 143 of them remarried

construction_notes: The register analysis is reported in the text only: the paper prints no table, no figure, no standard errors and no significance tests for any of the quantitative statements (section 'THE QUANTITATIVE SETTING – A REGISTER DATA ANALYSIS OF REMARRIAGE PATTERNS', pp. 161-162 (PDF pp. 6-7)).
The register results are presented here as a summary; the paper states that 'These results – which revealed a distinct pattern – are explained in full elsewhere (Liversage 2021)' (p. 161; PDF p. 6).
Remarriage shares are cumulative over the 16 calendar years 2003-2018 rather than annual rates.
Age differences are reported as ranges across the three immigrant groups (5-9, 10-15 and 14-20 years by type of new spouse), not as single coefficients.

Qualitative material: interviews in 30 families with a §94 self-appointed-helper arrangement (more than 100 interviews, in Danish, Arabic, Turkish or Urdu), 52 municipal care managers or other municipal actors, plus interviews with older immigrants and kin in families without a §94 arrangement; only five cases of substantially younger marriage migrant wives of older husbands were relevant for this article (pp. 160-161; PDF pp. 5-6).
The main qualitative case (Bouchra / Abu Mahmoud) rests on repeated visits over seven months, interviews with the wife, the husband and one adult daughter interviewed twice (p. 162; PDF p. 7).

claims.statement: Remarriage is rare among older immigrants in Denmark: of the almost 11,000 Turkish immigrants in the 55- to 80-year age group, only 143 (1.3%) remarried in 2003-2018.

definition.value: Whether a previously married (widowed or divorced) individual remarried during the observation window; reported as the share of the age group who remarried in the years 2003-2018 (143 of almost 11,000 Turkish immigrants = 1.3%). claims.statement: Care needs of older immigrant men in Denmark that are met neither by public eldercare (for linguistic and cultural reasons) nor by their adult children lead the men or their children to seek substantially younger wives abroad, who then perform the care work, in part remunerated as municipal §94 self-appointed helpers – a hybrid arrangement the authors call 'migrant carer-wives' and Danish care managers call 'fetched wives'.

treatment.label: unmet care needs of an older immigrant man (public eldercare unacceptable or inaccessible, adult children unable to provide the care)

definition.value: In the main case: an immigrant man in his mid-70s with several chronic conditions who lost the wife who had cared for him; rotating care by his six adult children failed because they were in full-time work or education and he insisted on staying in his own home; municipal home help failed because he could hardly communicate in Danish and refused to let female home helpers see him naked due to a cultural taboo. Established through qualitative interviews, corroborated by 52 municipal care managers.

timing.value: before and at the time the marriage is arranged; interviews conducted in the AISHA project, 2017-2021

outcome.label: marriage to a substantially younger migrant wife who provides in-home care (a 'migrant carer-wife' arrangement, part-remunerated through the §94 self-appointed helper scheme)

definition.value: A transnational marriage in which a substantially younger woman from the Global South arrives in Denmark, lives with and cares for her much older husband, with the exchange of care for money explicitly agreed (in the main case in an Islamic marriage contract specifying mahr and monthly remittances) and with the wife taken on as her husband's §94 self-appointed helper by the municipality for a small monthly salary.

timing.value: after the marriage and the wife's arrival in Denmark; the main case covers the first five years in Denmark (arrival 2016), other cases up to 10 years of marriage

magnitude.interpretation: 'From a marriage market perspective, the demand for such marriages indicates that care needs of the men involved are not presently met' (abstract, p. 156 (PDF p. 1)); the authors expect such arrangements to be rare: 'We expect that only a minority of these men have large care needs, so we believe that carer-wife arrangements such as Bouchra’s are rare.' (p. 166; PDF p. 11)

estimand.target_population: ethnic minority families in Denmark with an ageing immigrant man in need of care, in particular families using the §94 self-appointed helper scheme
estimand.time_horizon: the arrangement from the arrangement of the marriage onward; interviews 2017-2021, cases covering up to about 10 years of marriage

population.description: Ethnic minority families in Denmark interviewed in the AISHA project: 30 families with a §94 self-appointed helper arrangement (more than 100 interviews), 52 municipal care managers or other municipal actors, and older immigrants and kin in families without a §94 arrangement; five cases involved substantially younger marriage migrant wives of older husbands
population.selection: families recruited through use of the §94 self-appointed helper scheme, which the authors say meant a focus on families with substantial care needs; only five cases of substantially younger marriage migrant wives of older husbands were relevant

identification.source_of_variation: none – a directed content analysis of qualitative interviews in families with a §94 self-appointed helper arrangement and with municipal care managers; no exogenous variation and no counterfactual comparison group

key_assumptions.assumption: Informants' accounts of how and why the marriage was arranged describe the arrangement accurately; the authors rely on triangulation across the wife, the husband, an adult daughter and municipal care managers rather than on external validation.

claims.statement: Being a migrant carer-wife to a much older husband leads to isolated and strenuous lives with many care duties and to a precarious dependency on the husband's adult children, who do not necessarily regard their father's new wife as kin.

treatment.label: being a migrant carer-wife: a marriage migrant wife, substantially younger than her husband, living with and providing in-home care for him (in these cases as a §94 self-appointed helper)

definition.value: A woman who migrated to Denmark through family unification to marry a substantially older immigrant husband with care needs, performing his personal and household care; in the cases presented she is also paid a small monthly salary as his §94 self-appointed helper and has no worker rights such as maximum hours or days off.

timing.value: after arrival in Denmark and throughout the marriage; the main case describes her first five years in Denmark, another case 10 years of marriage

outcome.label: precarity: isolation, strenuous and unbounded care duties, and dependency on the husband's adult children (including over residence, inheritance and motherhood)

definition.value: Documented in the interviews as: being tied to the home almost around the clock with no friends or family; no maximum working hours or weekends off; no worker protection guaranteeing minimum pay or time off; limited access to the privileges of wifehood (a 'no inheritance' clause, prevention of motherhood); and fear of what will happen when the much older husband dies, given dependence on his adult children for navigating the Danish authorities.

timing.value: during the marriage, and prospectively at the husband's death

magnitude.interpretation: 'While these marriages may provide such women with a livelihood, they also lead to not only isolated and strenuous lives with many care duties but also a precarious dependency on the adult children of husbands, who do not necessarily regard their fathers’ new wives as kin.'
